## From rules to a prediction

Association rules **describe** what goes together. A model **predicts** something for one basket.

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[Rules]{.card-title}

Unsupervised. No Y column.

Output: *beer and cigarettes co-occur at lift 1.7*
:::
::: {.card}
[Model]{.card-title}

Supervised. You pick the Y.

Output: *this visit has a 22% chance of an in-store purchase*
:::
:::

Same gold table, **one row per basket or visit**, plus a label.

## Picking a label

A good label is three things:

- **Actionable.** Someone changes a decision because of the prediction.
- **Knowable in time.** You have the features *before* the outcome happens.
- **Not rare to the point of uselessness.** A 0.1% event needs a different approach than a 30% one.

::: {.takeaway}
**Write the sentence first:** "Given _____, predict _____, so that _____ can _____." If you can't finish it, you don't have a label yet.
:::

# Example: does fuel predict an in-store purchase?

## The setup

**Given what we know at the pump, will this customer also buy inside?**

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.card}
[The label]{.card-title}

`in_store` — did the visit include anything other than fuel?

**15.4%** of fuel visits do.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.card}
[The features]{.card-title}

Gallons, dollars, fuel grade, payment type, pump, hour, day of week, store
:::
:::
:::

A visit stitches transactions from the same shopper and store within 30 minutes, so the pump and the counter land in one row.

[**Example conclusions** — one run on the Idaho sample, not a finished analysis.]{.muted style="font-size:0.65em"}

## Fuel grade moves the number

| Grade | Fuel visits | In-store attach |
|---|---|---|
| Diesel | 6,536 | **21.5%** |
| Premium | 12,388 | 16.9% |
| Mid / Plus | 10,085 | 15.3% |
| Regular | 74,452 | 14.7% |

Diesel buyers are **half again as likely** to come inside. Worth asking why — trucks, trip length, time of day?

[**Example conclusions** — one run on the Idaho sample, not a finished analysis.]{.muted style="font-size:0.65em"}

## So does the size of the fill

| Gallons | Fuel visits | In-store attach |
|---|---|---|
| Under 5 | 14,418 | **18.4%** |
| 5 to 10 | 30,371 | 17.7% |
| 10 to 15 | 31,312 | 13.8% |
| 15 to 25 | 22,165 | 13.2% |
| 25 and up | 5,195 | 13.4% |

**Backwards from the guess:** small fills attach *more*. A quick top-up looks like a different trip than a full tank.

[**Example conclusions** — one run on the Idaho sample, not a finished analysis.]{.muted style="font-size:0.65em"}

## The strongest signal is a trap

| Payment | Fuel visits | In-store attach |
|---|---|---|
| Cash | 29,620 | **21.6%** |
| Credit | 73,841 | 13.0% |

::: {.takeaway}
**Cash customers walk inside to pay.** The feature isn't predicting behavior, it's describing the mechanics of the sale.
:::

Still useful for *counting* who comes in. Useless for *persuading* anyone to come in.

[**Example conclusions** — one run on the Idaho sample, not a finished analysis.]{.muted style="font-size:0.65em"}

## Leakage is the trap here

::: {.takeaway}
**If the in-store items are in your features, your model will be perfect and useless.** Filter them out of X before you aggregate.
:::

The same goes for anything that only exists *because* of the outcome: the basket total, the payment amount, the receipt line count.

[Ask of every feature: **would I know this before the customer walked in?**]{.orange}

# Other labels worth building

## Same table, different question

| Label | Type | Why a business cares |
|---|---|---|
| In-store purchase with fuel | Classification | Sizing the inside-sales opportunity |
| In-store spend, given a visit | Regression | What a converted fuel customer is worth |
| Basket total | Regression | Staffing, promotion lift |
| Visit includes foodservice | Classification | Prep volume, waste |
| Fuel grade chosen | Classification | Price elasticity by segment |
| Returns within 30 days | Classification | Retention, loyalty targeting |
| Visits per shopper per month | Count | Customer value, churn risk |

## The retention label

**52% of shoppers appear more than once**, across two years of data (Sept 2022 to Aug 2024).

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[Label]{.card-title}

Does this shopper return within 30 days?
:::
::: {.card}
[Features]{.card-title}

Last visit's basket, fuel grade, daypart, days since prior visit, visit count to date
:::
::: {.card}
[The hard part]{.card-title}

Picking the cutoff date so features come only from **before** it
:::
:::

This one forces a time-based split, which is the most common thing teams get wrong.

[**Example conclusions** — one run on the Idaho sample, not a finished analysis.]{.muted style="font-size:0.65em"}

## Rules can become features

The itemsets from FP-Growth are features for a model:

- Did the basket contain a **frequent itemset** we found?
- How many of the top 20 itemsets does it match?
- Basket size, category count, and the lift of the strongest rule it contains

::: {.takeaway}
**Unsupervised output makes good supervised input.** That's the honest reason to do both.
:::

## Judge the model against the base rate

With a **15.4%** label, a model that always says "no" is **84.6% accurate** and worth nothing.

- Report **lift over the base rate**, or precision and recall at the threshold you'd act on.
- Decide the threshold from the **cost of acting**: a coupon printed at the pump is cheap, a staffed offer is not.
- Check calibration: if you say 30%, does it happen 30% of the time?

[**Example conclusions** — one run on the Idaho sample, not a finished analysis.]{.muted style="font-size:0.65em"}

## What's under the data

- **Shopper IDs cover 29.6% of transactions**, and look card-based. Cash-only customers are mostly invisible.
- Only **5 stores** have payment and shopper records, out of 167.
- Visit stitching uses a 30-minute window; almost all of the effect lands within 15.

::: {.takeaway}
**Say this out loud in your presentation.** Knowing who is missing from your table is part of the result.
:::
